transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, thank you for fitting me in. I, um... I guess I'm just here because I've been noticing some habits lately that are really starting to bother me, and I felt like I needed to talk to somebody about it. 

You see, I'm a construction supervisor, which means I'm managing crews, dealing with contractors, handling material delays—basically putting out fires all day long. I'm on site from the crack of dawn, and then, on top of all that, half the time I have to go to these tense neighborhood meetings in the evenings to smooth things over with the locals about noise complaints or road closures. It’s just... it's a lot of pressure, and I'm usually the one who has to have it all together and be totally in control. 

But what made me actually bring it up and make this appointment is what happens when I finally get home. After those really long days on site, or especially after a draining neighborhood meeting, I’ll walk through the door and I just... I eat way, way more than I ever meant to. It’s like a switch flips. I’ll start with whatever leftover takeout is in the fridge—like half a pizza or some cold noodles—and then I just keep going. I'll pour myself a massive bowl of cereal, then I'm tearing into bags of chips, just... whatever’s there, honestly. I'll just keep eating and eating until I’m so uncomfortably full that my stomach actually hurts and I can barely sit right. It's just so frustrating because I manage a whole job site all day, but I get home and I just completely lose it around the pantry, you know?
When you find yourself eating a lot after coming home, do you feel like you're not in control of your eating, like you can't stop once you start?

Yeah, exactly. It’s exactly like that. It’s like... well, honestly, it feels like I’m completely on autopilot. I’ll be standing there in the kitchen, and the whole time, my brain is just screaming at me. I'm literally having this internal monologue where I'm telling myself, "You need to stop, you have to be up at 4:30 AM to meet the concrete guys, you need to go to sleep." I know I have an early crew start. I *know* it. 

But it's like my hands aren't listening to my brain. I'll put the bag of chips away, close the pantry door, and walk away, and then... I don't know, two minutes later, I'm right back in the kitchen going for more. It's so bizarre because at work, if I tell a crew to halt, they stop. I have total authority. But in my own house? I just can't seem to hit the brakes. I just keep going back and back, even when I'm exhausted and just wanting to sleep. 

It’s like someone else takes over the steering wheel, and I'm just sitting in the passenger seat watching myself eat. And then I think about how tired I'm going to be the next day on site, and you really need your wits about you when you're around heavy machinery and managing all those moving parts, you know? You can't be foggy. But even knowing all the risks and knowing how bad I'll feel, once I start on those evenings, I just... I really can't stop. I just keep going back to the kitchen.
After these episodes of eating a lot, do you ever try to compensate for it by making yourself sick, using laxatives, exercising a lot more than usual, or skipping meals?

Well... yeah. It’s really hard to say out loud, but... yes. Not every single time, but maybe, I don't know, a few times a month? 

It’s just that after one of those nights where I completely lose control and eat everything in the kitchen, I get this overwhelming, crushing sense of panic. You have to understand, in my line of work, especially being a female supervisor on a construction site, there is just so much pressure to command respect from the minute I step out of my truck. I put a massive amount of effort into looking sharp, looking capable, looking totally put-together. If I show up looking sluggish or bloated, or like I don't care, people notice. The contractors notice, the crew notices, and you can't show weakness or let them think you're slipping. 

So I'll be sitting there on my couch, my stomach just absolutely aching from all the food, and my brain starts racing a mile a minute. I start obsessing over how I'm undoing all the work I’ve put into looking put-together and professional. I think about my uniform fitting too tight, or my face looking puffy at the 6 AM briefing, and the panic just builds and builds until I feel like I'm going to jump out of my skin. 

So... on those really bad nights, a few times a month, I’ve gone into the bathroom and... well, I make myself throw up. I just feel like I have to undo what I just did. I have to get it out so I don't ruin my appearance or lose that edge I need for work. I just panic so much about all that effort going down the drain because of one stupid night in my kitchen. It's exhausting, honestly, but in that moment, I just can't sit there with the food inside me and the panic in my head.
How often do you find yourself making yourself vomit after these eating episodes, and does it happen only after particularly large binges or more regularly?

Well, if I really sit down and think about it... if I look back over the last few months, it's probably averaging out to about once a week. But it's not like a strict schedule, you know? It's not like every Friday night at 8 PM I'm doing this. It really fluctuates depending on what's going on at the site or with those neighborhood meetings. 

Like, there was this one week last month where we had a massive concrete pour scheduled, and the weather forecast was constantly changing, and the supplier was being a total nightmare, dodging my calls. I was so stressed out, I think I came home and lost control, and then threw up, maybe twice that week. I just couldn't handle the pressure of it all, and the panic of looking bloated in front of the crew on top of the concrete mess was just too much. 

But then, you know, we'll have a week where things are actually running smoothly, the weather holds, the contractors actually show up on time, and I might not do it at all that week. I might just come home, have a normal dinner, and go to bed. 

So it's not every single time I overeat, but it definitely happens after those really large, out-of-control binges where my stomach is just in knots and the panic is so loud I can't even hear myself think. It's just... it's a cycle, and it averages to about weekly, but it's so tied to the chaos of my job. And in construction, chaos is pretty much the only constant, so it feels like I'm always on the edge of it happening again. I just never know what kind of week it's going to be, so I never know how bad it's going to get at home.
Outside of your work concerns, do these eating episodes or the behaviors afterward cause you distress in other areas of your life, like with your family, relationships, or your sense of self-esteem?

Well... I mean, yes and no. Like, I'm still showing up. I haven't missed a single day on site. I'm still there at 4:30 AM, clipboard in hand, making sure the crew knows exactly what's expected of them for the day. I haven't let it touch my actual performance, because I just can't afford to. But... outside of the actual work hours? It's definitely starting to bleed into things, and it really bothers me. 

Like, my self-esteem takes a massive hit, obviously. I'll be standing in the mirror after one of those nights, just looking at myself, and I feel so... I don't know, ashamed? Weak? Here I am, this woman who can coordinate a massive commercial build, handle dozens of contractors, deal with city inspectors who are always looking for a reason to shut us down... and I can't even handle a bag of chips in my own kitchen. It makes me feel like a total fraud. 

And socially... it's definitely changing how I interact with people. We have these community meetings sometimes, you know, when we're doing a big residential development and we have to hear out the neighborhood's concerns about noise or traffic or dust. Usually, after those meetings, a few of the project managers or some of the local business owners will want to grab a bite to eat or get a drink to decompress. And I used to go! I used to enjoy it, building those relationships, talking shop off the clock. 

But lately... I've started turning them down. I'll make up some excuse about having to review blueprints or needing to be up early, even if I don't. I just... I get this anxiety that if I go out and eat with them, I might eat too much, or I might get triggered, or I'll just be thinking about the food waiting for me at home. So I rush home instead. I just want to get back to my house because I'm so worried the evening will get away from me, and if I'm at home, at least I can try to control my environment. But then I end up at home alone, and the cycle just starts all over again anyway. It's incredibly isolating, honestly. I'm pulling away from the networking and the social parts of my life just to manage this... this thing I'm doing in my kitchen. And it really sucks, because I've worked so hard to build a life and a career that I'm proud of, and I feel like I'm hiding this huge, messy secret from everyone.

Can you describe what it feels like right before one of these eating episodes starts? Do you feel like you have a choice about whether to start eating, or does it feel like you can't control it from the beginning?

It's... well, it's a few different things happening all at once. Like, I'll be driving home from the site, right? And usually, my phone is ringing off the hook the entire drive—subcontractors asking about material deliveries for the next morning, or my boss needing an update on the framing timeline, or somebody complaining about a permit issue. So my brain is just completely keyed up. By the time I actually pull into my driveway, turn off the truck, and walk through the front door, the silence in my house is almost deafening. 

I'll kick off my work boots—they're usually covered in mud or drywall dust, depending on what phase of the build we're in—and I just feel this immense, heavy exhaustion, but at the same time, there's this weird, buzzing anxiety right under my skin. I'll walk into the kitchen, maybe just intending to grab a glass of water or a normal snack, you know, just something small to tide me over. I'll tell myself, "Just a quick bite, you need to wind down and relax." 

But then... I don't know, it's like a switch flips in my brain. The second I take that first bite, any sense of having a choice just completely evaporates. It's gone. Once I start on those evenings, it literally feels like I’m on autopilot. It's the strangest feeling, almost like I'm watching myself from the outside. I'll be standing there, tearing into packages, and in my head, my inner voice is practically screaming at me to stop. I'm literally telling myself, "You have to stop doing this, you have an early crew start tomorrow, you need to get to sleep, you're going to feel terrible on site." I know my alarm is going to go off at 3:45 AM and I need to be sharp for the morning safety briefing. 

But it's like my body just completely disconnects from my brain. I can be thinking all those logical things, but I'm still just going back to the kitchen for more. Back to the pantry, back to the fridge, opening cupboards, just grabbing whatever is there. It's terrifying, honestly. Because, like I said, I'm a supervisor. I make a hundred critical decisions a day, I direct dozens of guys, I control heavy machinery schedules and million-dollar budgets... but in my own kitchen, standing in front of my own fridge, I have absolutely zero control. The autopilot just takes over completely, and I can't snap myself out of it no matter how hard I try to reason with myself.
Outside of these eating episodes, do you ever feel like you're not in control of yourself or your actions in other parts of your life?

Well, no... if I really sit and look at my life, it's actually the exact opposite. Everywhere else, I am completely, one hundred percent in control. I mean, I have to be, right? With my job, I'm managing a site with maybe forty, fifty guys on any given day. Plumbers, electricians, drywallers, heavy machinery operators... if I'm not in absolute control of every moving part, the whole project falls apart and we lose tens of thousands of dollars a day. 

Just last Tuesday, for example, we had this massive issue where the framing crew received the wrong gauge steel studs for the load-bearing walls on the second floor of this new commercial build. And the supplier tried to say it was my fault, but I had the purchase orders right there, meticulously organized in my binder. I had to step in, shut down the floor, reroute the electricians to the first floor so they wouldn't lose a day's pay, and get on the phone with the supplier to force them to hot-shot the right materials out to us by noon. I didn't even blink. I just handled it. I directed traffic, I made the calls, I solved the problem. People look to me for direction constantly, and I never freeze up or lose my grip on the situation. 

So, yeah, I'm very decisive. I manage my finances down to the penny, my truck is spotless, my tools are organized, my project schedules are color-coded... I don't drink too much, I don't gamble, I don't do anything reckless. I don't have any other areas where I just let go of the wheel. 

That's why this whole food thing is so incredibly frustrating and confusing to me. It makes absolutely no sense. How can I be the person who can coordinate a crane delivery in downtown traffic without breaking a sweat, but I can't stop myself from tearing through my pantry when I'm alone in my own house? It's like there are two completely different people inside my head. The work me is this hyper-competent, totally in-control supervisor, and the home me is just... I don't know, completely unhinged, but only with the food. Literally nothing else. It's just the kitchen. It's so weird, isn't it? I just don't understand how the wires get so crossed when I'm so disciplined everywhere else.
Can you recall any situation outside of these eating episodes where you’ve felt the same kind of lack of control over your actions, even briefly?

No, honestly... no. I really can't think of a single time. I mean, I was actually just thinking about this the other day, trying to figure out if there's some kind of pattern, you know? Trying to see if maybe I'm just an impulsive person in general. But I'm not. Like, even in situations where most people would completely lose their temper or just act on impulse, I don't. I'm always the one keeping a lid on things. 

Just to give you an idea, last month we had this city inspector who is notorious in our district for being incredibly difficult. He showed up completely unannounced on a Friday afternoon, right when we were trying to wrap up the rough-in plumbing inspection for a three-story build. And he just started nitpicking everything. Things that were totally up to code, he was questioning. He was condescending, he was holding up my guys who just wanted to go home to their families, and I could feel my blood boiling. I was so incredibly angry, and part of me just wanted to snap at him, to just lose it and tell him off because he was being so unreasonable. 

But I didn't. I didn't even come close to losing control. I just took a deep breath, pulled out the approved schematics, and very calmly, very methodically walked him through every single pipe and fitting until he had no choice but to sign off on it. I didn't yell, I didn't act out... I stayed completely in the driver's seat. 

And that's how I am with everything. Even when I'm dead tired, or furious, or stressed out of my mind, I never get that... that feeling like someone else is steering the ship. I always know exactly what I'm doing and I always have the brakes. So, no, I've never felt that autopilot thing anywhere else. Not in arguments, not with money, not with drinking... nowhere. It's literally just when I'm standing in my kitchen at night. And that's what drives me so crazy about it! It's like, if I can handle a hostile city inspector trying to shut my site down on a Friday without losing an ounce of control, why on earth does a box of crackers completely defeat me? It just doesn't make any sense.
Have you ever experienced a similar loss of control over eating in situations outside your home, such as at a restaurant, at work, or during a social event?

No, actually, never. That's the thing that makes it all so incredibly baffling to me! If I'm out at a restaurant with friends, or if we're doing a working lunch on the site—like, sometimes I'll order pizzas for the framing crew if we hit a major milestone ahead of schedule, or I'll just grab a quick sandwich from the food truck that comes around to the industrial park—I eat totally normally. I'll have a couple of slices, or eat my sandwich, and I'm just done. I don't even think twice about it. I can sit at a table full of appetizers at a social event, like a holiday party or a vendor dinner, and just have one or two things and walk away. There's absolutely zero panic, zero feeling of being overwhelmed. I'm completely present and in the moment.

It really is just like I was trying to explain a minute ago. It is strictly tied to my house, at night. It's like, once I start on those specific evenings, when I'm finally alone in my own space... that's when it feels like I’m completely on autopilot. Like I was saying, I'll literally be standing there, actively telling myself to stop because I know I have an early crew start and I need to be sharp for the safety briefing, but I'm still just turning right back around and going back to the kitchen for more. 

It's like the logical part of my brain just gets locked out of the control room, but only when I'm standing in my own house. Out in the real world, at a restaurant or a bar or a job site? Totally fine. I can leave half a burger on my plate and not even care, or watch a plate of fries sit there and not touch them. But at home, on those evenings... it's just that endless loop of going back for more no matter how much I yell at myself in my head to stop and go to bed. It's like a geographic curse or something, I swear. I just don't get why the location changes everything.
Have you ever experienced one of these eating episodes when you weren’t feeling particularly stressed or overwhelmed, like on a calm, uneventful day?

You know, I really don't think so. I'm trying to think of one, but... well, to be completely honest, a calm, uneventful day is a pretty rare commodity in my life right now. But even when I do get them, no, I don't think I've ever had that happen. 

Like, if I really sit back and look at a genuinely relaxed day—let's take last Sunday, for example. It was actually a really great day. I didn't have to go down to the site at all. I actually put my work phone on silent for a few hours, which is something I almost never do, but the framing was totally finished on Friday and we were just waiting on the drywall crews to start Monday morning, so I knew there were absolutely no fires to put out. I spent the whole morning just out in the driveway detailing my truck. That's kind of my therapy, honestly. Just taking my time, getting all the drywall dust out of the air vents with a little detailing brush, washing the undercarriage, putting a good coat of wax on it. It was quiet, the weather was perfect, I wasn't rushing to be anywhere. Then I went to the hardware store for a few things for the house, came back, made a regular dinner, and just watched some football on the couch. 

And on a day like that? Nothing. Absolutely nothing. I didn't have that weird, frantic urge to keep eating. I didn't find myself wandering back into the kitchen. I just ate my normal dinner, put my plate in the dishwasher, and that was the end of it. The kitchen was just a normal room in my house again. 

It really seems like it only happens when I've got that... that residual hum of stress from the job site vibrating in my chest, you know? Like on a Tuesday or a Thursday when I've been running around for twelve, fourteen hours, dealing with sub-contractors who didn't show up, or trying to decipher some vague city ordinance, and my brain has been running at a million miles an hour all day. Then I finally get home, the door shuts, and the quiet is almost... I don't know, almost too loud? It's like my brain doesn't know how to power down from being in high-alert supervisor mode, and that's when the wheels come off. But if I'm already having a calm day, where I'm just moving at my own pace and I'm not carrying the weight of a multi-million dollar build on my shoulders? No, I really can't remember a single time it's happened then. I'm trying to rack my brain to see if maybe it happened on a vacation or a holiday, but honestly, no. If I'm actually relaxed, I'm just... normal.
When you start eating during these episodes, does it feel like you are making a choice to keep eating, or does it feel like you are completely unable to control yourself from the moment you begin?

It definitely doesn't feel like a choice. Not at all. I mean, maybe the very first thing I grab—like if I decide to have a handful of chips or a bowl of cereal right after I finally get my work boots off—maybe that very first bite is a choice. But the second I finish it? That's when the switch just flips. 

It’s exactly like I was trying to explain earlier, honestly. Once I start on those evenings, it just feels like I am completely on autopilot. There's no conscious decision-making happening anymore, which is what makes it so terrifying. It's so frustrating because my logical brain is still awake in there, you know? Like, I'm literally standing in my kitchen, and I am actively telling myself to stop. I'll be thinking, "You have an early crew start tomorrow, you need to be up at 4:30 AM, the concrete trucks are arriving at 5:30 and you need to be sharp." I know all of this. I'm literally reciting it in my head. I'm telling myself to just walk away, go upstairs, wash the drywall dust off my face, and get in bed. 

But even while I'm having that entire rational argument with myself, I'm still just turning right back around and going back to the kitchen for more. It's like my hands and my mouth are operating completely independently from my brain. I'll be opening a box of something, knowing I shouldn't, knowing I'm going to feel exhausted and sluggish on the site the next day when I need to be keeping an eye on fifty different guys and heavy machinery, and I just... I can't make myself put the box down. The brakes just stop working. So, no, it really doesn't feel like a choice to keep going. It feels like I'm just a passenger in my own body watching it happen, completely unable to intervene.

Have you ever felt this same kind of loss of control with anything other than eating—like with spending, driving, or other actions—where you felt like you couldn’t stop even though you knew you should?

No, actually... no. Not at all. And honestly, that's another thing that makes this whole situation so incredibly frustrating and just... confusing to me. Because if you look at literally every other area of my life, I am probably the most disciplined, in-control person you'll ever meet. 

Like, with spending? I manage multi-million dollar budgets for these builds. I am the one tracking material costs, making sure we don't go over on lumber or copper wiring, auditing the subcontractor invoices... and I am meticulous about it. And even in my personal life, I'm exactly the same. I don't just go to a store and black out with a credit card, you know? I track my personal expenses on a spreadsheet. I saved up for years to buy my truck so I wouldn't have a crazy car payment. If I go to the hardware store for a specific drill bit, I buy exactly that drill bit and I leave. There's no impulse buying, no losing control whatsoever. 

And driving? Oh my gosh, definitely not. I drive a heavy-duty pickup, and half the time I'm towing a flatbed trailer full of equipment or materials. You absolutely cannot zone out or lose control when you're hauling a skid steer down the interstate at sixty-five miles an hour. I'm hyper-aware behind the wheel. I've never even had a speeding ticket! I'm constantly checking my mirrors, anticipating what other drivers are doing, leaving plenty of braking distance... I'm always the designated driver if I go out with friends because they know I don't take risks. I don't drink too much, I don't gamble, I don't do anything reckless. 

My whole life, my whole career, is built on being the responsible one. I'm the supervisor. I'm the one making sure fifty different guys are wearing their PPE and tying off on the scaffolding and following safety guidelines to the absolute letter. I am always in the driver's seat, literally and figuratively. So to have this one, bizarre, isolated thing where my brain just completely short-circuits in my own kitchen... it just makes absolutely no sense to me. If I had some kind of generally impulsive personality, you'd think it would bleed over into my finances or my driving or something, right? But it doesn't. Everything else is completely locked down and managed. It's just... it's just the food. I just don't understand why I can manage a massive construction site down to the last penny, but I can't stop myself from opening another box of crackers.
Have you ever had one of these eating episodes when you weren't alone at home—like if a friend or family member was staying over, or if you were with someone after work?

No, never. Never, ever. And honestly, I think that’s a huge part of why I feel so crazy about the whole thing, because if someone is around, it’s like... it’s like it’s not even an option in my brain. 

Like, just a couple of weeks ago, my younger sister was passing through on her way to Denver, so she crashed in my spare room for two nights. And I was completely fine. We actually ordered a pizza the first night, which is usually something that might trigger a whole thing for me if I were by myself, but with her there? I just had two slices, a side salad, and that was it. We sat on the couch, watched a movie, drank some sparkling water, and I didn't even *think* about going back into the kitchen to keep eating. The urge just completely vanished, or maybe the fact that she was sitting right there just totally neutralized it. It was the same thing the next morning—we had normal breakfast, I went to work, came back, we made chicken and vegetables, and again, totally normal. 

It’s the same way if I have one of the project managers over to go over blueprints, or if I’m out at a work dinner with the suppliers. I eat a normal portion, I stop when I’m full, and I don't give it a second thought. I think... I think it’s because I am just so absolutely terrified of anyone seeing me like that. Like I was saying, I’m the boss. I’m the one who has everything together, the one who solves the problems. The idea of anyone—even my own sister, who I love to death—watching me just mindlessly shoving handfuls of cereal or stale crackers into my mouth, completely unable to stop myself... it literally makes my stomach turn just thinking about the embarrassment. 

So if there is another breathing soul in my house, or if I'm out in public, that "supervisor" mask is firmly in place. I am totally in control. It’s only when the front door locks, the deadbolt clicks, and I know for an absolute, one-hundred-percent fact that nobody is coming over and nobody is watching... that’s when the walls come down and the whole thing starts. If there's any chance of being seen, the brakes work perfectly fine. So no, it has never happened when I wasn't completely alone. I just couldn't bear the shame of it, you know?
During these eating episodes, do you feel like you are completely unable to stop eating, even if you wanted to, from the moment you start?

Yeah, I mean, it's exactly like I was trying to explain a few minutes ago. It really is. Once I start on those evenings, it just feels like I’m on total autopilot. It's like the logical part of my brain gets completely disconnected from my body. 

I'll be standing right there, literally telling myself to stop because I have an early crew start the next morning. I'll be running through my whole schedule—you know, thinking about how I need to be on-site before the sun is even up, how the concrete guys are going to be waiting on me to unlock the gates, how I need to be sharp and focused for the safety briefings... I'll be thinking all of that, practically begging myself to just go upstairs, wash up, and go to sleep. 

But even while I'm having that whole rational argument in my head, I'm still going back to the kitchen for more. I'm reaching for another box or another bag, and I just can't stop my hands from doing it. Even though I want to stop more than anything, and I know how awful I'm going to feel the next day on the site, I just... I can't. The control is just completely gone.
Is it always the case that you only feel completely unable to stop eating when you're alone at home, and never when you're with someone else or in a different setting?

Yeah, it really is always the case. It's exactly like I was just saying—if there is anyone else around, in any other setting, I am perfectly fine. I have total restraint. But when it's just me, at home, that's when it all just completely falls apart. 

Once I start on those evenings, it just feels like I’m on total autopilot. I mean, I'll be standing right there in the kitchen, literally telling myself to stop because I have an early crew start the next morning. I'll be going over the whole morning schedule in my head, knowing I have to be the first one to unlock the gates, check the weather for the concrete pour, make sure all the safety gear is laid out for the new guys... and I'm actively telling myself, "You need to stop, you need to go to bed, you have to be up and functioning in four hours." 

But even while I'm having that exact thought, even while I'm practically begging myself to just walk away, I'm still going back to the kitchen for more. It's the strangest, most frustrating thing in the world. It's like my brain knows exactly what I should be doing, but my body just won't listen to me, and I just keep reaching for another box of whatever is in the pantry. But if my sister were sitting on the couch? Or if I was at a diner with the project managers? That autopilot switch never even flips. It's only when I'm completely alone in my house that I totally lose that ability to stop myself.

Is the loss of control you feel during these episodes limited only to eating, or have you ever experienced similar feelings of being unable to stop yourself with other behaviors, even if just briefly?

I... no, it's just the eating. I mean, I really try to keep a tight ship in every other area of my life. Like I said, I'm a supervisor on a construction site, so I have to be the one who is completely dialed in. I have to manage the schedules, coordinate the sub-contractors, make sure the materials are delivered on time, handle the safety inspections... I mean, if I lost control on the job, people could get seriously hurt, or we could lose thousands of dollars in delays. So I am very, very disciplined when it comes to work. 

And even with other things, like... I don't know, drinking or shopping or whatever else people might lose control over. I'm not like that. I might have a beer with the crew after a long week, but I'll literally have just one and then switch to water because I know I have to be up early to review the blueprints for the next phase. I stick to my budget, I pay my bills on time, I keep my truck maintained... I am honestly a very responsible, controlled person in literally every other aspect of my life. 

That's why this whole eating thing is just so baffling and frustrating to me. It's like I have this one weird, isolated glitch in my system. I can manage a multi-million dollar construction project without breaking a sweat, but I can't stop myself from eating an entire sleeve of cookies when I'm alone in my own kitchen. It makes absolutely no sense. But no, to answer your question, I don't have that feeling of being unable to stop with anything else. It's just... it's just the food. And only when I'm alone.
Do these eating episodes cause you a lot of emotional distress, such as feeling upset, disgusted with yourself, or very worried about what this means about you as a person?

I... no, not really. I wouldn't say I feel disgusted with myself or, you know, worried about what it means about me as a person. I mean, I'm just not really wired like that to begin with. I don't sit around analyzing my soul or spiraling into some deep emotional crisis over it. 

Like I was saying, I'm running a crew of forty-plus guys, dealing with heavy machinery, sub-contractors, weather delays, safety inspectors breathing down my neck... I just don't have the time or the luxury to get all wrapped up in emotional distress. It's honestly more just... intensely annoying. Like a logistical problem. When I wake up the next morning, I'm not looking in the mirror crying or feeling ashamed of my character. I'm just irritated because my stomach hurts or I feel sluggish, and I know I have to climb up scaffolding or walk the site for twelve hours in the heat. 

It's exactly like if a piece of equipment breaks down on the site—like, if the excavator throws a track, I don't cry over the excavator, I don't think it means we're terrible people, I just get mad that it's slowing down our timeline and creating more work for me.
